title: The hypertrophy series: the hypertrophy rep range conundrum
summary: NH argues that no single hypertrophy rep range like 8-12 exists; any rep range grows muscle if it brings enough stress. The practical range is whatever reaches maximum recoverable volume efficiently, safely and quickly, which rules out very heavy singles and very high-rep light work as staples. Varying rep ranges, like varying implements, is itself a form of intensity variety.

claims.claim: There's no such thing as a hypertrophy rep range: singles, 8-12 or 20-rep sets all build muscle if they bring the muscle to fatigue.
Practically, the hypertrophy range is whatever achieves maximum recoverable volume as efficiently, safely and quickly as possible.
Powerlifters still grow from low-rep work, but lower total tonnage means they gain more strength than size; bodybuilders using high reps with real weight end up bigger relative to their strength.
Successful powerlifters don't just do 1-3 rep sets; they train various ranges because they also need muscle size.
For hypertrophy, pick rep ranges that yield maximum tonnage from working sets inside a good intensity window, neither too easy nor too hard.
Only doing 8-12 reps, however many sets, isn't optimal; muscles need to experience a variety of rep ranges and intensities.
Intensity isn't only weight: lift variation, bar type and supersets also change it.
Some muscles respond better to high reps and some to low, and some shouldn't be trained heavy for injury reasons; it's individual.
His hamstrings respond well to high reps and have high endurance, so he gives them lots of sets and reps and avoids low reps for them.
A rep range is just part of the recipe for tonnage; how you reach the tonnage doesn't matter as long as the sets challenge you.
10 sets of 1 with very heavy weight is high-quality tonnage but impractical and risky; 3 sets of more reps at 70-85% gives similar tonnage more feasibly and safely.
Very high reps with very light weight is boring, doesn't drive progress, is limited by cardiovascular endurance, and would take about 5 hours if applied to every body part.
Extreme low or high rep work can supplement training but shouldn't be the bread and butter for size.
